lessons.n1:
IP addresses and ports

An IP address identifies a machine on a network. A port identifies a service on that machine. Together they form an endpoint: 203.0.113.10:443.

The ports you will meet constantly

22    SSH
53    DNS
80    HTTP
443   HTTPS
5432  PostgreSQL
8080  a dev server

Loopback

127.0.0.1 (or localhost) always means "this machine". A service bound to 127.0.0.1 is reachable only from the box itself; bound to 0.0.0.0, it listens on every interface — including the public one.

ip addr        show your interfaces and addresses
"It works locally but not from outside" is almost always a service bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, or a firewall rule.
lessons.n2:
DNS: turning names into addresses

Humans use names; routers use addresses. DNS is the lookup that bridges them.

dig labdeck.dev

dig labdeck.dev.	300	IN	A	203.0.113.10

Read that answer as: the name labdeck.dev maps to an A record with address 203.0.113.10, and the answer may be cached for 300 seconds (the TTL).

Record types

  • A — IPv4 address
  • AAAA — IPv6 address
  • CNAME — an alias pointing at another name
  • MX — mail server
  • TXT — arbitrary text, used for verification and policy

When it fails

NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist. A timeout means the resolver could not be reached. Both look like "the site is down" from a browser, and both are diagnosed with dig.

DNS is cached at every layer — browser, OS, resolver. A change you made a minute ago may not be visible yet. That is the TTL doing its job.
lessons.n4:
HTTP, headers and curl

HTTP is a request and a response. The response has a status line, headers, and optionally a body.

curl -I https://labdeck.dev

HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000

Status codes worth knowing

  • 200 OK · 301 moved permanently · 304 not modified
  • 401 unauthenticated · 403 forbidden · 404 not found
  • 500 server error · 502 bad gateway · 503 unavailable

Headers that matter

strict-transport-security tells the browser to always use HTTPS. x-content-type-options: nosniff stops MIME sniffing. cache-control decides how long a response may be reused.

curl -I https://labdeck.dev     headers only
curl https://labdeck.dev        the body
-I sends a HEAD request. It is the fastest way to answer "is this endpoint alive, and what is it serving?"
lessons.n6:
ping, traceroute and listening ports

Three commands cover most "it is not reachable" investigations.

ping — is the host alive?

ping labdeck.dev

64 bytes from 203.0.113.10: icmp_seq=1 ttl=57 time=9.8 ms
4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss

100% packet loss means the host is down, or ICMP is blocked. It does not prove the service is down — a host can answer ping and still refuse connections.

traceroute — where does it stop?

traceroute api.labdeck.dev

Each line is a hop. Latency that jumps at one hop points at that network, not at your server.

ss — what is actually listening?

ss -tulpn

tcp LISTEN 0.0.0.0:443   users:(("nginx",pid=101))
tcp LISTEN 127.0.0.1:5432 users:(("postgres",pid=104))

This is the ground truth. If nothing is listening on 443, no amount of DNS fixing will help.

Order of investigation: DNS resolves → host answers → port is listening → service returns 200. Each step rules out everything below it.
